title: Julia Kristeva
keyWorks: Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection (1980)
The Sense and Non-Sense of Revolt (1996)
Female Genius — a trilogy on Hannah Arendt, Melanie Klein and Colette (1999–2002)
summary: Julia Kristeva is a philosopher, linguist, psychoanalyst and novelist who came to Paris from Bulgaria in 1965 and became one of the central figures of poststructuralism. She coined the term “intertextuality,” showed how bodily rhythm and the strict order of meaning meet in language, and wrote books on abjection, love, melancholia and the stranger who lives in each of us. Kristeva teaches us to see in the darkest and most “awkward” feelings not a breakdown but the work of the boundaries from which our “I” is made.
onEmotions: Kristeva distinguishes two layers in the psyche. The “semiotic” is ancient and bodily: rhythm, pulse, intonation, drives that live in us before words. The “symbolic” is language, rules, names, meaning. A feeling is born where the two meet, and much suffering, for Kristeva, is experience that has not yet found its signs. Her main path is not to suppress a feeling but to translate it into form: a word, a story, an image, music. For her a person is a “subject in process,” never finished. Even disgust, which she called “abjection,” and black melancholia are described without judgment — as ways in which a fragile “I” builds and guards its boundaries.

anxiety.text: An infant knows no words yet but already startles, cries and quiets to a lullaby — Kristeva would start here. Exhausting anxiety lives largely in that pre-verbal layer and doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. Kristeva distinguished two layers in our psyche. The “symbolic” is words, grammar, plans, the names of things. The “semiotic” is an older layer: rhythm, tension, pulse, intonation, everything that lives in the body before words. Anxiety, from her point of view, is like a semiotic wave that hasn’t yet found its words: your heart pounds, something inside goes round in circles, and you can’t name it. Kristeva spoke of the human being as a “subject in process”: we are never finished, and tension is part of that movement. As a psychoanalyst, she cared about something else too: an experience becomes easier to bear when it is gradually translated into signs — into words, images, a story. Not to cancel it, but to give it a place.
anxiety.practice: Hum any simple tune with your mouth closed for a minute, feeling the vibration in your chest and face. Give the anxiety a rhythm, since it has no words yet.

fear.text: Behind one clear image a whole crowd of nameless worries sometimes hides — Kristeva saw this as the psyche at work, not the psyche broken. Your fear is an ancient and honest feeling; it protects what you hold dear. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva examines Freud’s famous case of Little Hans — a boy who was afraid of horses. She shows that the object of a phobia can be like a condensation: many vague fears that have no name of their own gather into one clear image. The horse frightened him not only as a horse — it carried a whole tangle of anxieties. Take Kristeva’s thought one step further, and it turns out that adult fears are sometimes built the same way: a concrete occasion — a conversation, a doctor, a journey — takes on the weight of something much wider. That doesn’t make the fear imaginary. But if you gently ask what else is sounding in it, it often becomes more understandable and a little less all-powerful.
fear.practice: Imagine your fear as Little Hans pointing at the horse, and gently ask: “What else is frightening here?” Listen for the first word that comes.

sadness.text: “The black sun of melancholy” — a line by Nerval that Kristeva made the title of her book on sorrow: a light that doesn’t warm, yet still shines. You don’t need to be ashamed of sadness, or hurry it on its way. In it, Kristeva offers an unexpected view: sorrow is not only pain but also a kind of support. When something inside falls apart, sadness gathers a person into one whole feeling: heavy, perhaps, but whole. It seems to say, “There was a loss here, and it matters.” Kristeva saw the way forward not in suppressing sadness but in giving it form — in words, music, drawing, conversation. It’s no accident that her book is full of readings of artists and writers — Holbein, Dostoevsky, Nerval, Duras — who turned sorrow into signs. When sadness takes on a form, it stops being mute and becomes part of your story.
sadness.practice: Sit for five minutes in dim light and let the sadness be — without explaining it or chasing it away. If you like, hum something quiet.

grief.text: Holbein’s Dead Christ — the painting a Dostoevsky hero says could make you lose your faith — is at the heart of a chapter of Black Sun: Kristeva looks at how art withstands a direct gaze at loss. Grief is love with nowhere left to go, and it keeps no proper timetable. There Kristeva also describes how language itself is born. A child can say “mama” because mama is sometimes not there: the word appears where we come to accept absence. Kristeva puts it almost as a paradox: I have lost what is most precious, but because I have agreed to lose it, I can find it again in signs. For someone grieving this is not a substitute consolation: signs do not bring a person back. But they let you keep your bond with them — in stories, words, names, rituals. From Kristeva’s point of view, grief that finds its speech does not become less than love; it becomes love’s continuation.
grief.practice: Say aloud the name of the one you lost and one sentence addressed to them. Words are born where we meet absence — let yours be heard.

loneliness.text: Just before Christmas 1965, a young Bulgarian scholar named Julia Kristeva landed in Paris — by her own account with almost no money and no acquaintances. Loneliness can be very sharp, and it doesn’t prove that no one needs you. Years later she would write in Strangers to Ourselves about the particular experience of the foreigner: living between languages, feeling that you are never quite heard. But the book’s central idea — following Freud and his notion of the “uncanny,” something at once familiar and strange — is that the strange lives inside each of us. We don’t coincide even with ourselves. Kristeva might say that loneliness is not your personal flaw but a heightened version of the common human condition: we are all a little foreign. Paradoxically, this shared condition can become a bridge: someone else may be lonely in just the same way.
loneliness.practice: Call or drop in on someone you can be quiet with — and simply spend five minutes together, without necessarily talking about anything important.

anger.text: Mallarmé broke syntax the way you break an old frame — and Kristeva saw in this the same force that lives in our anger. Anger is a powerful energy, and you don’t need to hide it from yourself. Kristeva did not divide the drives into “good” and “bad.” In Revolution in Poetic Language she writes about “negativity” — the destructive, rejecting force of the drives, without which there is neither growth nor creativity: for something new to appear, something old must be thrown off. Poets like Lautréamont and Mallarmé, as she saw it, let precisely this force into language and broke the usual order of sentences. It doesn’t follow that anger should be poured out on people. What follows is something else: anger has a form in which it can be lived through without harm — rhythm, movement, a sharp word on paper. Anger that has found its form often tells you which boundary you want to protect.
anger.practice: Stamp your feet or drum your palms on your knees in a strong rhythm for a minute — give the anger a semiotic outlet. Then say one word that names it exactly.

shame.text: “Don’t touch, that’s not nice” — for Kristeva, phrases like this build our “I” from childhood as something “clean and proper”: the French propre means “clean,” “proper” and “one’s own” all at once. We learn to draw boundaries: what in me is acceptable, what must be hidden. Shame, one of the most tormenting feelings, makes you want to vanish from other people’s eyes. Kristeva would probably note that shame flares up when that boundary seems to have been breached: something out of place has broken out, and it has been seen. But her analysis shows something else as well: these boundaries are largely set by culture, and the “improper” exists in every human being. Shame speaks of a boundary, not of your worth.
shame.practice: Place your palm where the shame lives right now — face, chest, belly — and hold it there as you would hold someone cold. Say: “This is me too.”

guilt.text: The ancients washed away defilement with water and ritual, while modern people carry it inside — Kristeva traced this path from ritual to conscience. Guilt can be a heavy burden, and the fact that you feel it already speaks of your conscience. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva traces how culture has dealt with what it considered “impure.” In the biblical prescriptions, defilement is external: it is set apart by rules and prohibitions. In Christianity, by her analysis, it moves inward and becomes sin — and with that comes the possibility of putting it into words: repentance, confession, forgiveness through speech. Later, in Black Sun, Kristeva writes of forgiveness not as forgetting the deed but as the gift of a new meaning: what was done is not erased, but it can be given a different continuation. Without drawing religious conclusions, you can take the essential point: guilt is eased not by silent self-punishment but by words.
guilt.practice: Wash your hands slowly, as a small rite, and silently name what you are ready to answer for and what it is time to rinse away. Guilt that has words is lighter.

envy.text: An infant at a breast that doesn’t feed as fast as it wants — Melanie Klein began her account of envy with this scene, and Kristeva wrote a whole book on Klein. Envy is an unpleasant but deeply human feeling: those who admit it feel it, and so do those who don’t. Following Klein, she sees envy as one of the earliest feelings: a wish not so much to get someone else’s good thing as to spoil it, because it isn’t mine. Klein and Kristeva speak of this without moralizing. What matters is that envy has a counterweight — gratitude, the capacity to take in what is good and rejoice in it. The two feelings don’t exclude each other: when we notice envy without condemning ourselves, we often make room both for gratitude and for understanding what we are actually missing.
envy.practice: Name aloud one good thing the person you envy has, then add: “And I have…” — finish with something of your own. Klein considered gratitude the antidote to envy.

emptiness.text: Words feel like cardboard, desires are gone, and emptiness can be worse than pain — Kristeva, a practising psychoanalyst, heard such confessions many times and wrote about them with great respect. She spoke of the “Thing” — a loss older than any concrete loss, which cannot be named because it happened before we learned to speak. When this ancient emptiness rises, signs lose their weight: a person speaks, but the words stop meaning anything. Kristeva described it as a broken link between words and feeling. What helps then? From her point of view, the way back begins with the semiotic — with what comes before words: rhythm, melody, color, the voice of someone close. You don’t have to find the meaning of life right away. It’s enough for something small to start sounding again.
emptiness.practice: Put on a song you loved as a child and listen without thinking about the words — only melody and rhythm. Emptiness sometimes needs not meaning but rhythm.

confusion.text: Kristeva changed country, language and profession — from linguist to psychoanalyst, from scholar to novelist — and knew what it is like when your old picture of the world stops working. Confusion is frightening, but there is nothing shameful in it. For Kristeva, a human being is a “subject in process.” The French phrase carries a double meaning: en procès means both “in process” and “on trial,” that is, in question. Our “I” is not a finished statue but constant movement between a stable order of words and meanings and the living forces that wear that order away. In Revolution in Poetic Language, Kristeva shows that it is precisely in moments of disruption, when familiar language can no longer cope, that something new is born. Kristeva might say that confusion is not a breakdown but a transition: the old form no longer holds, and the new one is still coming together.
confusion.practice: Imagine yourself a year from now, looking back on these days, and ask: what process began back then? Don’t answer right away — just hold the question.

fatigue.text: A lullaby, the sound of rain, a steady walking pace — Kristeva would remind us that the psyche needs not only the right words but rhythm. Fatigue is not laziness but a signal from the body worth listening to. We have not only a “symbolic” life — roles, duties, the right words — but also a “semiotic” one: the rhythm of breathing, the pulse, the need for quiet and repetition. Living only in the symbolic is exhausting: you constantly have to measure up, explain, keep up appearances. It seems that deep fatigue is the voice of the semiotic layer, long left without attention and now demanding its own rhythm. It asks not for new meanings and tasks but for simple repeated things: rocking, warm water, quiet music. Rest, in this logic, is not a reward for work done but a return to your own rhythm.
fatigue.practice: Lie down for five minutes and listen only to your breathing — not improving it, not counting. Let the symbolic wait while the semiotic rests.

boredom.text: A question Kristeva would ask: do you have time today to be alone with your own soul — without a feed, a series, a ready-made answer? Boredom can be sluggish and dreary, and it too is saying something. In New Maladies of the Soul, Kristeva writes about the modern person surrounded on all sides by ready-made images and standard answers. There is neither time nor room to build an inner life of one’s own — what she called “psychic space.” Kristeva would probably note that boredom is the sensation of a language the rhythm has drained out of: everything has been said in advance, everything is the same, nothing pulses. Her remedy is not new entertainment but a return to the living word. It’s no accident she valued poetry so highly: in it, sound, repetition and surprise are joined to meaning again. Boredom can become an invitation to listen for what in you has not yet been said.
boredom.practice: Read one line of a favorite poem aloud, slowly, listening to the sound rather than the meaning. Notice where the pulse returns to language.

joy.text: Kristeva wrote a book on Colette — a writer who could rejoice in the smell of a garden, a cat, a ripe peach as if each were a whole event. Joy is a beautiful state, and it needs no justification. She was also one of the first to introduce French readers to Mikhail Bakhtin and his idea of carnival — a festival where laughter suspends hierarchies and familiar roles. In her own theory, joy, laughter and music are moments when the semiotic — bodily, rhythmic — breaks freely into the ordered world of words and rules. She has a word for such moments: jouissance — enjoyment, fullness, when the boundary between “I” and the world becomes permeable for an instant. Kristeva did not consider this frivolous: without such flashes the symbolic order would turn to stone. Joy, then, is not a distraction from life but its renewal.
joy.practice: Like Colette, describe aloud one thing that delights you in three sensations: color, smell, sound. Say them slowly, savoring each word.

love.text: Narcissus by the stream, Romeo beneath the balcony, a troubadour singing to an unattainable Lady — in Tales of Love Kristeva travels through the whole history of love, from Plato to psychoanalysis. Love is one of the strongest experiences there is, and it has every right to turn a life upside down. Her central idea: falling in love is a crisis and a renewal of the “I.” In love our boundaries open, our former identity wavers, and we rebuild ourselves around an ideal. Kristeva compared the psyche to an “open system” — a living organism that renews itself only in exchange with another. She does not debunk love as an illusion, although she sees narcissism and idealization in it too. On the contrary, she considers this capacity to shed one’s skin beside another person one of the foundations of a living psyche.
love.practice: Say aloud one thing you have started seeing differently since you fell in love. That is the sound of a renewed “I.”

gratitude.text: A well-fed infant falls asleep with such trust that Melanie Klein saw in it the first image of gratitude. It is a warm, gathering feeling, and you want it to last. In her book on Melanie Klein, Kristeva examines Klein’s thinking about gratitude in detail. For Klein it is not politeness but a deep capacity: to receive something good from another, let it inside, and allow it to become part of yourself. Gratitude, for Klein, is the counterweight to envy: where envy spoils the good because it belongs to someone else, gratitude lets it simply be. Kristeva valued this idea because it shows that good things don’t only happen to us — we learn to receive them. So your gratitude is no small thing: it is a sign that there is a place inside you where good can come in and stay.
gratitude.practice: Recall something good you received today and hold that memory for a minute, as if placing it inside you in a warm spot. Then say quietly: “Thank you.”

hope.text: A child’s first word is already a small act of trust: the child believes it will be heard, and Kristeva could see in such small things the beginning of hope. Holding on to fragile hope is not naive. In This Incredible Need to Believe, Kristeva, who called herself a non-believer, argues that the need to believe is universal and older than any religion. It is born in early childhood, when an infant trusts that it will be heard, that its cry will be answered, that it is being held. Kristeva calls this stage trust in a loving other, present in the child’s world before any rules. If so, hope is not a calculation of odds but a continuation of that first trust: faith that the world is capable of answering. You can protect it even when the evidence is thin. It rests not on a forecast but on the experience that once, you were already held.
hope.practice: Say aloud to the empty room one sentence about what you hope for — as if you will certainly be heard. Notice how your breathing changes.

nostalgia.text: The smell of a stairwell, a tune from an old phone — sometimes a single sensation is enough to bring back a whole year. Nostalgia is a sweet, aching longing for the past, and Kristeva knew where all its tenderness comes from. In Time and Sense, Kristeva wrote about Proust — the author in whom the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea suddenly gives the narrator back a whole childhood. She was interested in how a sensation — a taste, a smell, a sound — keeps time better than conscious memory does. This is close to her idea of the semiotic: we have a layer of experience recorded not in words but in rhythms, shades, bodily imprints. It seems that nostalgia often longs not so much for events as for this fabric of sensations. And that is why the past is not entirely lost: it lives in the body and answers when it meets a familiar smell or melody.
nostalgia.practice: Find one sensation from the past today — a smell, a taste, a song — and live it slowly, like Proust with his madeleine. Don’t analyze; just remember with your body.

craving.text: The hand reaches out by itself, before any thought — Kristeva would look for the source of that movement where there were no words yet. A sharp “I want it now” can feel almost irresistible, and weakness of character has nothing to do with it. In Black Sun, Kristeva speaks of the “Thing” — an ancient, nameless lack older than any particular desire. Later, in New Maladies of the Soul, she writes about how the modern person tries to plug this lack with quick fixes — shopping, images, substances — so as not to meet it face to face. Kristeva would probably note that a craving promises to restore a lost fullness instantly. But a substance or an object cannot be what it seems: it only screens the emptiness for a while. What helps is not fighting yourself, but trying to understand what exactly the craving promises, and looking for another, gentler way to express it.
craving.practice: Ask yourself: “What feeling am I hoping to get right now — calm, warmth, oblivion?” Name it, and notice how the wave of craving rises and gradually subsides.

addiction.text: In her consulting room Kristeva listened to people for whom a substance or a screen had taken the place of words — and never looked down on them. Addiction is not a moral failure, and shame only adds to the weight. In New Maladies of the Soul, she describes a person whose “psychic space” has shrunk — the inner place where pain, desire and loss can become a thought, an image, a word. When there is little of that space, suffering seeks an immediate outlet, and a substance or a habit begins to do the work that speech and close relationships would otherwise do. The path her thinking suggests is to gradually restore that space: to learn to name what hurts, and to share it with those who are able to listen. It is long work, and it doesn’t require you to be perfect.
addiction.practice: Write down in one sentence what feeling the addiction helped you hide from. If you’d like, you can talk about it with people who know this path from the inside — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: In the morning your body feels foreign, and you want to move away from it — Kristeva knew this movement and gave it a name. The morning after calls for gentleness, not a verdict. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva describes “abjection” — an ancient movement of rejection, when we push away from ourselves whatever threatens our boundaries: the nauseating, the unclean, the “not right.” It follows that a hangover is often experienced exactly like this: as if your own body and last night had become “not mine,” and you want to distance yourself from them. The revulsion speaks of breached boundaries, not of you being a bad person. Kristeva believed the abject can be dealt with not only by casting it off but also through words. To gently name what happened is to take your body back.
hangover.practice: Wrap yourself in a blanket, put a palm on your belly and breathe for a minute, as if warming someone who feels awful right now. No verdicts until lunchtime.

euphoria.text: Kristeva has an untranslatable French word for such moments — jouissance: an overflowing enjoyment in which the boundary between “I” and the world becomes permeable, like a child laughing until they hiccup. A burst of euphoria, when everything seems possible, can be beautiful, and you don’t need to be suspicious of it straight away. She described it as a breakthrough of the semiotic — rhythm, energy, bodiliness — through the usual order. This is not frivolity: without such breakthroughs there would be neither music nor poetry. But Kristeva always showed that the semiotic lives in a pair with the symbolic — word, form, coherence. So a good way to live a high more fully is to give it form: say it, write it, sing it. Then the joy won’t just rush through you — it will stay with you.
euphoria.practice: Spin or jump to a favorite song until you laugh. Then stand still and feel the rhythm fading in your body.

crash.text: Kristeva loved rhythm — in poems, in lullabies, in breathing — and every rhythm has a rise and a fall. A sharp drop after a celebration, a success or a substance can feel like a fall, but it is not the truth about you, nor proof that everything good was a lie. Kristeva might say that the psyche lives in constant oscillation: now a semiotic wave — energy, rhythm, rapture — dissolves boundaries, now the symbolic gathers them again — with rules, tasks, the heaviness of words. The crash is the return of boundaries after they have opened, and it can be painful, like light after darkness. But in the “subject in process” Kristeva saw movement, not a final state. Neither the rise nor the fall is the last chapter. The joy that was there remains real.
crash.practice: Read any poem aloud slowly and notice how your voice rises and falls in each line. The fall is part of the rhythm, not its end.

panic.text: A mother rocks a crying infant, and its breathing gradually falls into her rhythm — Kristeva saw in this the most ancient form of comfort. A panic attack is one of the most frightening experiences there is: a wave of terror washes over you, your body seems to stop obeying, and it really is very frightening. Kristeva described how, in moments of intense terror, the familiar order of words and meanings — the symbolic — seems to retreat, leaving the bare semiotic: pulse, breath, trembling. It seems that in panic the body speaks its ancient language of rhythm. That is why what helps is not arguing with the terror but a gentle return to simple supports: a slow rhythm of breathing and the most ordinary words — the names of things around you. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. There is nothing you need to decide right now — just breathe and wait for it to pass.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, gently rocking back and forth as in a cradle. Quietly name the colors around you aloud — rhythm and word together.

dread.text: “I am the dark one, the widower, the unconsoled,” begins Nerval’s sonnet, which Kristeva reads as a map of human despair and of the way out. The sense of an abyss, of “what is all this for,” comes to thoughtful people, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva describes the place “where meaning collapses”: encounters with what threatens the very boundary of our existence. But her book is not about surrendering to horror. She shows how people in every age have answered it: with ritual, with religion and above all with art. Literature, from Dostoevsky to Proust and Joyce, in her view, knows how to look at horror and give it form — and in that there is purification, catharsis. From her point of view, meaning is not given to us once and for all, but we create it again and again — through speech, creativity, bonds with others. That work is itself the answer to the abyss.
dread.practice: Read aloud one line of poetry you love, and repeat it three times, slowly. Meaning is made again and again through speech — even over the abyss.

fomo.text: Someone else’s holiday, someone else’s party, someone else’s flawless kitchen — Kristeva would call it a shop window with not a single real soul visible behind it. The feeling that real life is happening somewhere without you is painful. In New Maladies of the Soul, Kristeva writes about a person besieged by a stream of images. The screen offers ready-made pictures of other people’s lives, and less and less room is left for one’s own inner life — for dreams, doubts, unhurried reflection. She called this inner place “psychic space.” Take Kristeva’s thought one step further, and it turns out that the fear of missing out appears when other people’s images begin to replace your own experiences: we compare our complicated lives with someone else’s curated frames. The remedy here is not to fit more in, but to reclaim your right to your own inner time, which nobody photographs.
fomo.practice: Close your eyes for two minutes and recall in full detail one moment of your own today — a sound, a smell, someone’s voice. This is your “psychic space,” and it is no worse than other people’s pictures.

sleepless.text: When the lights go out, sounds, rhythms and vague images return first — Kristeva knew that this is how the earliest layer of the psyche works. A sleepless night drags on, thoughts in the dark seem heavier than by day, and it is not your fault. Kristeva would probably note that at night the symbolic weakens — the daytime order of plans, tasks and proper words — and the semiotic rises to the surface: scraps of images, rhythms of anxiety, vague sensations of the body. That’s why night thoughts are so hard to reach with logic: arguing with them by reasoning is useless. Kristeva reminded us that our first supports were rhythmic — a voice, rocking, a lullaby. The psyche still responds to this ancient language. Instead of solving daytime problems at night, you can give yourself a simple rhythm. Conclusions reached at night are not necessarily true: in the morning, much looks different.
sleepless.practice: Lying in the dark, slowly stroke the blanket with your palm in the rhythm of calm breathing. Let the semiotic get a lullaby instead of new thoughts.

betrayal.text: The house where you slept without a lock suddenly turns out to be open to strangers — that, for Kristeva, is what a blow to the very boundaries of the self feels like. Betrayal wounds especially deeply, because the blow comes from where you felt safe. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva notes something striking: abjection — a deep, almost bodily revulsion — is provoked not only by filth but also by the traitor, the liar, the criminal with a clear conscience. Because they reveal the fragility of what we relied on: law, agreement, trust. Kristeva helps us understand why betrayal is felt not simply as sadness but as nausea, as if the ground had gone out from under you. Your reaction is proportionate: the boundary your sense of safety rested on has been destroyed. But this speaks of the other person’s act, not of your naivety. Trusting is not a mistake; it is the foundation of living with people.
betrayal.practice: Wrap your arms around yourself and feel where the boundaries of your body are — shoulders, back, palms. Say: “My boundaries are still here, even if trust is wounded.”

jealousy.text: Narcissus looked into the stream and saw himself — Kristeva thought that in love we too look into a mirror, only the mirror is the other’s eyes. Jealousy can burn very fiercely, and it doesn’t make you a bad person. In Tales of Love, Kristeva shows that in love we build our “I” around the other: their gaze and attachment become a mirror in which we see ourselves as loved and significant. She isn’t embarrassed by the word “narcissism”: for her it is a necessary foundation of any love. Kristeva might say that jealousy is the fear that the mirror will turn toward someone else, and your image of yourself will shatter along with it. Hence its sharpness: what is under threat is not only the relationship but who you feel yourself to be. It helps to reclaim at least part of your footing — what is valuable in you regardless of anyone else’s gaze.
jealousy.practice: Look in a mirror for a minute and name aloud one thing you value in yourself regardless of anyone else’s gaze.

resentment.text: For Kristeva, a living psyche keeps asking the past questions — and resentment is a question too, one that was never answered. It is heavy because you were treated unfairly. In The Sense and Non-Sense of Revolt, Kristeva speaks of “revolt” in the old sense of the word: as a return, a re-examination, a question we put to the past. For her such revolt is a condition of a living psyche: without it a person freezes. Following Kristeva, two paths can be distinguished. Resentment goes round in circles, repeating the same thing. Revolt returns to the wound in order to question it and find a new meaning. This doesn’t require forgiving what cannot be forgiven. But moving from repetition to questioning can gradually loosen resentment’s grip and give you back your movement.
resentment.practice: Ask your resentment one question aloud, like a rebel in the old sense of the word: “What do you want me finally to understand?” Listen to what the silence answers.

heartbreak.text: Love, for Kristeva, is like a building site: around another person, the “I” builds itself anew. A broken heart hurts almost physically, and that is no exaggeration. In Tales of Love, Kristeva describes love as a state in which the “I” opens up and rebuilds itself around another. So a breakup is not only the loss of a person: the version of yourself you built together with them collapses too. And in Black Sun she shows that each new loss can awaken older, earliest losses — hence the feeling that it hurts more than it should. That is simply how the psyche is made. But there is hope here too: the capacity for love that opened you to another doesn’t disappear. If you were once able to rebuild yourself beside someone, that capacity remains yours.
heartbreak.practice: Put a hand on your chest and feel your heart keeping its rhythm — steady, stubborn. Tell it: “We keep building.”

impostor.text: At twenty-five Kristeva coined a word every literary scholar now knows — “intertextuality” — and it is unexpectedly comforting for anyone afraid of being found out: “I’m an impostor, and soon everyone will realize.” Following Bakhtin, she showed that every text is woven from other texts: it absorbs other people’s words and makes them its own. Take Kristeva’s thought one step further, and it turns out that a person is built the same way. Your skills, manners and thoughts were gathered from teachers, books, colleagues — and this is not forgery but the ordinary way meaning exists. The impostor thinks that somewhere there are “real” people, made out of nothing. But there are none. The difference is not whether what you have is borrowed, but how you have combined and reworked what came from others.
impostor.practice: Name aloud three people you learned something from, and one thing you made your own out of it. That is your personal intertext.

quote.text: Any text is constructed as a mosaic of quotations; any text is the absorption and transformation of another.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva

self_hatred.text: Kristeva, a psychoanalyst with many years of practice, wouldn’t take the verdict “I am disgusting” at face value: for her it is not a fact but a symptom. When an inner voice keeps insisting you are good for nothing, it hurts terribly — and it is not telling the truth about you. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva describes “abjection” — an ancient movement of rejection through which every person, in childhood, learns to separate “I” from “not-I.” She notes that this movement can also turn against oneself: a person begins to push away parts of themselves. For Kristeva this is a mechanism common to all people, not a verdict. The voice of hatred is an echo of a very early way of building boundaries, not a considered assessment of your life. You can notice it as a phenomenon and not agree with it. And the psyche, for Kristeva, is always in process — it can be built differently.
self_hatred.practice: Choose one part of yourself you usually push away — a habit, a trait, a memory — and say to it aloud: “You’re mine too.” Nothing more.

helplessness.text: A knot that won’t come undone however hard you pull — Kristeva would suggest you stop pulling and call someone to help. Helplessness, the feeling that nothing depends on you, is one of the hardest feelings, and you don’t have to be ashamed of it. Kristeva, following Freud, reminds us that human life begins in complete helplessness. An infant cannot survive without someone to hold it. So vulnerability is not a defect but our shared foundation. Kristeva also wrote a great deal about this in connection with disability — including in an open letter to the President of France about people with disabilities (2003). Her idea: vulnerability makes us human and connects us to one another. From her point of view, you can see in helplessness not only a dead end but also a reminder that we are not meant to cope alone.
helplessness.practice: Ask someone for a small bit of help today — to open a door, give a pointer, stay nearby. Notice that asking is an action too.

procrastination.text: Mallarmé could sit over a single line for ages — Kristeva saw in such torment not laziness but a struggle between living rhythm and correct form. “I can’t get started” is easily mistaken for laziness, though most often that’s not what it is. Kristeva helps us see a conflict between two layers in it. The task lives in the symbolic: deadlines, requirements, the right form, evaluation. But the wish to do something is born in the semiotic — in interest, rhythm, a bodily “I want to.” When the symbolic presses too hard, demanding that you do it right and well from the start, the living impulse freezes. Studying poets like Mallarmé, Kristeva showed that the new is born where rhythm and sound at first run ahead of meaning. Kristeva might say that it helps to begin not with what’s correct but with what’s alive: a draft, a sketch, a clumsy first sentence that still has movement in it.
procrastination.practice: In two minutes, sketch by hand the clumsiest, most alive version of a start — arrows, scraps, scribbles. Let the semiotic begin before the symbolic.

uprooted.text: Living in a language you weren’t born into means translating yourself a little every day; Kristeva has done it all her adult life, ever since she moved from Bulgaria to France. Being torn from the places you come from is a deep loss. In Strangers to Ourselves, she describes the foreigner’s experience with great precision: life between two languages, the silence when your native words are of no use to anyone here and the new ones have not yet become your own. She doesn’t prettify this pain. But her key move is to turn the view around: the foreign is not only outside, it lives inside every person, even one who has never left home. Your rootlessness is not a deviation from the norm but a heightened experience of something everyone shares. And in that clarity freedom can appear: you are building yourself, not only inheriting.
uprooted.practice: Hum a song or lullaby in your native language, even if you remember only a couple of lines. The native rhythm lives in your body and hasn’t gone anywhere.

quote.text: Strangely, the foreigner lives within us: he is the hidden face of our identity.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva

overload.text: Where inside you, Kristeva would ask, is there still room for your own thoughts when your head is full of other people’s pictures? Overload is a real burden, not a personal weakness. In New Maladies of the Soul, Kristeva describes the modern person being filled with images without being given time to process them. She speaks of the shrinking of “psychic space” — the inner place where impressions turn into one’s own thoughts and feelings. When the stream is too dense, impressions are not absorbed but simply pile up as noise. From Kristeva’s point of view, the way out is not to consume faster, but to reclaim the pause. One impression truly lived through and named gives more than a hundred scrolled past.
overload.practice: Turn off the screen and look at one still object for five minutes — a cup, a plant, a window. Let your psychic space widen a little.

unreality.text: Everything is visible and understood, yet nothing touches you, as if there were glass between you and the world — that is how Kristeva in Black Sun describes the state in which words and things lose their weight. The feeling that the world, or you yourself, is not quite real can be strange and unsettling, and it deserves gentle care. She explains this as a break in the link between signs and feelings. From Kristeva’s point of view, the way back runs through the semiotic — through the layer of experience older than words: texture, temperature, sound, rhythm. It was simple sensations that first connected us to the world in childhood, and they can still restore a sense of presence. You don’t need to prove to yourself that everything is real — it’s enough to touch.
unreality.practice: Hold an object with a clear texture — wool, a stone, bark — and run your fingers over it for a minute, naming aloud: “rough,” “cool,” “warm.”

awe.text: Kristeva traveled to China, wrote about Saint Teresa and about Proust — and everywhere she looked for moments when a person meets something larger than themselves. Awe before mountains, a starry sky, great music is one of the most powerful experiences, and you want to keep hold of it. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva observes that the abject borders on the sublime: both go beyond the limits of our “I,” but where the abject threatens, the sublime expands us. It follows that in awe the “I” for a moment stops being the center, and this is not frightening but freeing: we find ourselves part of something larger than we know how to name. Words fall short — and that is as it should be: here the semiotic is speaking, the rhythm and breath of the world. Such moments don’t need explaining. You can simply allow them, and later remember them tenderly.
awe.practice: Put on one great piece of music and listen to the first three minutes standing, with your eyes closed. Let it be bigger than you.

relief.text: A spectator of ancient tragedy left the theater lighter than they came in — this was called catharsis, purification, and Kristeva thought the word describes relief well. The exhale after long tension deserves to be fully felt. In Powers of Horror, she shows how ritual and art helped people meet what threatened them, give it form — and come out renewed. Tension doesn’t vanish without a trace: it passes through us, and we end up on the other side. In other words, relief is the moment when boundaries that were under threat hold again, and the psyche can relax. Don’t rush straight on to the next task. Let your body notice that the danger has passed.
relief.practice: Take three deep exhales with sound — “haaa” — as after a long performance. Feel where your body let go of the tension.

calm.text: In the Timaeus Plato speaks of a mysterious “chora” — the nurse and receptacle of everything that comes into being. Calm is worth cherishing without asking more of it, and Kristeva helps explain where it comes from — she used this word for the earliest space of our psyche: not yet words or thoughts, but rhythm, warmth, a voice, rocking, in which an infant feels held. Kristeva might say that deep calm is a meeting with this ancient layer: when nothing needs to be named or proven, and steady breathing and a quiet rhythm are enough. Such calm is not empty. It nourishes: words and deeds later grow out of it. You can simply be in it, without turning it into a task.
calm.practice: Sit comfortably, place a palm on your chest and for a minute listen to your breath rising and falling. Name nothing — just stay in the “chora.”

inspiration.text: Kristeva writes novels herself — and knows well how a sentence sometimes arrives before the plan, like a melody. Inspiration is a joyful surge, and you want to catch it. Kristeva explains what happens in it in her major theoretical book, Revolution in Poetic Language. There she shows how, in poets like Mallarmé and Lautréamont, the semiotic — rhythm, sound, bodily energy — bursts into the symbolic, into correct language, and remakes it from within. That is how the new is born: not from rules alone and not from pure chaos, but from their meeting. It seems that inspiration is the moment when living energy finds its way into form. Let it flow without demanding perfection straight away. You can tidy up the form later, but the flow is worth not letting slip.
inspiration.practice: For three minutes, write down whatever comes without correcting a word — let rhythm run ahead of meaning. Then underline one living phrase.

schadenfreude.text: When someone else slips, for a moment we feel steadier on our own feet — Kristeva would explain why. Schadenfreude, secret pleasure at someone else’s failure, is rarely admitted aloud though almost everyone feels it, and it says nothing final about you. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows that our “I” holds itself together on the boundary between “me” and “not me.” When someone falls, especially someone who seemed more successful or who hurt us, that boundary is strengthened for a moment: “it happened to them, not to me.” Kristeva would probably note that schadenfreude is a brief relief from our own vulnerability, which we glimpsed in another. If you notice this without condemning yourself, the feeling becomes a clue: where do you yourself feel fragile or undervalued? What matters is not the feeling itself but what you do with it.
schadenfreude.practice: Picture that person at their moment of failure and, in your mind, offer them a hand. Notice that your own steadiness hasn’t shrunk.

contempt.text: “The foreigner lives within us,” Kristeva writes, and this phrase unexpectedly turns contempt inside out. It can feel cold and reliable, like armor, and feeling it is human. In Strangers to Ourselves, Kristeva, following Freud, observes that what we push away with dislike in another often turns out to be our own unacknowledged strangeness. We wall ourselves off from “them” so as not to face what troubles us inside. Her conclusion: if we recognize the stranger in ourselves, we won’t have to hate it in others. Take Kristeva’s thought one step further, and it turns out that contempt guards a boundary — between “me, the decent one” and “them.” This doesn’t mean your judgment of another’s actions is wrong. But it’s worth asking what exactly the boundary is protecting — and then the armor may become a little less necessary.
contempt.practice: Name one trait that repels you in this person and honestly ask: where does it live in me, even in a tiny form? Just notice, without a verdict.

disgust.text: Your throat tightens, your hand pulls back — the body says “no” before the mind can think, and Kristeva listened seriously to that “no.” Disgust — at a situation, at people, even at yourself — is a strong bodily feeling, and there is nothing shameful in it. It is the central theme of Kristeva’s Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection. She calls it “abjection” and begins with a simple example: the skin on the surface of milk that makes a child shudder. Abjection, for Kristeva, is the most ancient way we separate “I” from “not-I”: we push away what mixes with us and blurs our boundaries. That is why disgust is provoked not simply by dirt but by the ambiguous, the in-between, what is out of place. This knowledge is freeing: your disgust is not a moral verdict but a signal about a boundary. And what to do with it is up to you.
disgust.practice: Take a step back from what disgusts you and breathe out slowly, as if pushing it away with your hand. Say aloud: “That is not me” — and feel that the boundary holds.

quote.text: It is thus not lack of cleanliness or health that causes abjection but what disturbs identity, system, order. What does not respect borders, positions, rules. The in-between, the ambiguous, the composite.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva
quote.source: Powers of Horror: An Essay on Abjection (1980)

revenge.text: Kristeva trusted the power of the word more than the power of a blow: naming a wrong is already the beginning of stopping it. The wish for revenge can burn, especially when the hurt is deep and unjust, and the wish itself is not a crime but a sign of great pain. Kristeva wrote a great deal about how the symbolic — law, speech, recognition — arises in culture as a way of translating destructive drives into something we can live with together. Revenge, then, often wants not so much to cause pain as to win recognition: for the wrong to be named as wrong, and for you to be seen as the one who was hurt. In other words, that recognition is better sought in words than in an act that would extend the chain of destruction. Your wish for justice is legitimate, and there are safer paths for it.
revenge.practice: Write a letter you will never send: what you would want this person to understand. Then keep it or tear it up.

anger_at_loved.text: A teenager slams the door on the mother they love more than anyone — Kristeva would see in this not ingratitude but growth. Anger at those closest to us — a partner, parents, children — happens to almost everyone, and so does the shame that follows. Drawing on Melanie Klein, Kristeva shows that love and aggression have been intertwined in our most important relationships since childhood: the person closest to us both demands the most of us and can hurt us the most. She stresses something else as well: to become a separate person, everyone has to separate from those they love, and there is inevitably anger in that separation. From Kristeva’s point of view, anger at someone you love is not proof that there is no love, but part of the living bond between two different people. What matters is that it finds its outlet in words, not in something that could wound.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger at someone close rises, step away for a minute and splash cool water on your face, feeling your own boundaries return. Then say one “I” sentence: “I’m angry because…”

ambivalence.text: Look at a person, Kristeva would suggest, like a painting that can’t be cut in half: its light and dark are painted with the same paint. To love and be unable to stand the same person at the same time is agonizing, but deeply human. In Tales of Love, Kristeva examines Romeo and Juliet and shows that even in the most famous love story, hatred stands beside desire — and this is no accident but part of the experience of love. And in her book on Melanie Klein she explains that the psyche matures when it stops dividing loved ones into “all good” and “all bad” and learns to hold both images in one person. Klein called this the “depressive position” — not an illness but a stage of maturity. So your mixed feelings are not a malfunction but a sign that you see the person whole.
ambivalence.practice: Picture this person whole — with what you love in them and what drives you mad — as one portrait. Hold the image for a minute, erasing no color.

guilty_relief.text: A watercolor in which two colors have run together doesn’t become dirty — it becomes alive; Kristeva looked at feelings in a similar way. Relief after someone leaves, after a breakup, or even after the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening: “How can I feel this?” But relief and love get along perfectly well together. In her book on Melanie Klein, Kristeva shows that love and heaviness, tenderness and weariness are always intertwined in close relationships. When long tension finally lets go, the psyche exhales — and that is not betrayal but the reaction of a living person who has carried a great deal. Kristeva would probably note that the shame here comes from wanting our feelings to be “pure,” all one color. But the psyche is never uniform. Relief does not cancel your love and grief — it speaks of how long you held on.
guilty_relief.practice: Drip a little tea and a little juice into a glass of water and watch them intertwine. That is how relief and love live side by side.

indifference.text: Ice on a river doesn’t mean there’s no water underneath — Kristeva would speak of indifference in much this way. When you aren’t moved by what “ought” to move you — an event, a tragedy, someone’s joy — it’s frightening: what if I have no feelings? But it doesn’t mean you are a bad person. In Black Sun, Kristeva describes how a psyche overloaded by pain or loss can muffle the link between words and feelings: a person understands what is happening but doesn’t feel it. She treated this with respect — as a defense, not a vice. Take Kristeva’s thought one step further, and it turns out that indifference often means not an absence of feelings but their freezing: there’s too much, and the psyche is protecting itself. Feelings come back not on command but gradually, through small, bodily, unhurried impressions.
indifference.practice: Hold a cup of warm tea in your palms for a minute and simply feel the warmth moving into your fingers. Feelings thaw slowly, and there is no need to hurry them.

escape.text: Kristeva once did what you may be dreaming of: she went where no one knew her and began a life in another language. The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your familiar role — can be very strong. In Strangers to Ourselves, Kristeva describes the foreigner sympathetically, as someone who once left their origins and gained a particular freedom for it: they are no longer defined only by where they come from. It follows that the dream of escape is a wish to become a “subject in process” again, not frozen in a single role. But she honestly shows the cost as well: a new place doesn’t cancel our inner strangeness — we take it with us. So it’s worth asking which role you want to leave behind — and where change could be let in right now.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I ran away, I could finally…” Then think about what tiny part of that you could try here.

forbidden_attraction.text: Forbidden fruit is sweet precisely because it is forbidden — Kristeva turned this old saying into a serious thought. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” can be confusing and unsettling, but in itself it decides nothing for you. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows that prohibition and desire are born together: a prohibition doesn’t just restrain desire, it outlines its object and lends it a special allure. And in Tales of Love she traces how culture, from the troubadours to Don Juan, has told again and again of love at the edge of the permitted. In other words, such attraction often speaks not only of the person but of what you are missing — freedom, recognition, aliveness.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Name aloud in one word the lack this attraction speaks of: freedom, recognition, aliveness. Think where you could add some of it to your life without the forbidden.

social_anxiety.text: Kristeva would suggest looking around the room and noticing: you are not the only one who feels awkward — everyone is a little bit of a stranger. Shyness and fear of other people’s eyes can make any social contact hard. In Strangers to Ourselves, Kristeva writes about the stranger — a person who feels out of place among others. Following Freud, she shows that everyone knows this feeling from the inside: in each of us there is something strange, awkward, something that doesn’t match the proper image. The people around you who seem so confident also carry this strangeness within them. From Kristeva’s point of view, shyness is not your personal defect but a sharp experience of a shared condition. If everyone is a little foreign, then being awkward among people is not the exception but the general rule — and you can forgive yourself for it.
social_anxiety.practice: At your next gathering, look for someone who also seems a little lost, and smile at them or ask a simple question. Two strangers side by side are already less strange.

quote.text: The foreigner is within me, hence we are all foreigners. If I am a foreigner, there are no foreigners.
quote.author: Julia Kristeva

uncertainty.text: A tree that doesn’t sway in the wind is probably already dead — Kristeva would say something like this about a psyche that has stopped changing. Uncertainty can be exhausting, and the wish for clarity is completely natural. Kristeva described the human being as a “subject in process” and liked to compare the psyche to an “open system” — like a living organism that exists only as long as it exchanges with the world and changes. A closed system looks stable, but it freezes. It seems that uncertainty is the price of openness: as long as you are alive and connected to others, the future cannot be fully known. That doesn’t make the anxiety pleasant. But it can shift your view: you don’t have to know how it will all end. It’s enough to stay open and take the next step.
uncertainty.practice: Go out for five minutes and watch the wind move the branches or the clouds change shape. Tell yourself: “I am a living open system too.”

waiting.text: Time in a doctor’s waiting room, by the phone, outside an exam hall — Kristeva would call it a special time: you are no longer where you were, but not yet where you are going. Waiting can be agonizing: time drags, and there’s nothing you can do. Kristeva uses the phrase “subject in process,” and in French it is ambiguous: en procès also means “on trial.” Kristeva would probably note that waiting feels so heavy because it resembles waiting for a verdict: as if the answer will decide who you are. But her idea is that the “I” is always in process, and no single decision will define it once and for all. The result may change a great deal in your circumstances, but not your worth. And while your body waits, you can give it its own rhythm — footsteps, breathing, a simple task.
waiting.practice: While you wait, swing your foot or tap your fingers in a slow rhythm, counting to sixty. Give your body its own rhythm, since time has frozen.

regret.text: Kristeva wrote a book on Hannah Arendt and especially valued her idea that a human life is a story that continues as long as we live — there is no last page while you are still breathing. Regret over what you did or didn’t do can keep coming back, and that is a sign that you cared. Arendt saw in forgiveness the capacity to release a person from the consequences of the past so they can begin anew. In Black Sun, Kristeva also speaks of forgiveness — not as forgetting, but as the gift of a new meaning to what happened. The past cannot be changed, but its place in your story can: instead of a final full stop, it can become a chapter after which something began.
regret.practice: In your mind, retell this story as if it were a chapter from the middle of a book, not the last one. What chapter could come next?

longing.text: A letter reread until it falls apart is the oldest way of giving longing a form, and Kristeva respected such forms. You can long for a particular person — their voice, their presence, your conversations — almost physically, and there is nothing excessive about it. In Tales of Love, Kristeva shows that a loved one becomes part of our inner world: we talk with them in our minds, they live in our imagination, in the way we look at things. Absence doesn’t erase this; it makes the inner bond sharper. It follows that longing is love that lacks a meeting, and it needs at least a form. Kristeva always emphasized that signs — words, letters, memories — are born in the place of absence. To give longing words is to give the bond a place where it can live.
longing.practice: In your mind, tell this person three things about your day, as if they were sitting beside you. Love that lacks a meeting needs at least a form.

world_pain.text: Kristeva believed that pain given a form — a word, a drawing, an act — stops merely pressing down and begins to mean something. Pain for the world from grim news, wars and injustice speaks of your capacity for compassion, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva notes that the horrifying both repels and attracts: we want to turn away — and can’t tear our eyes off it. This shows why an endless news feed is so draining: it holds us in this oscillation, letting us neither make sense of things nor grieve. Culture, for Kristeva, has always answered horror with form — ritual, art, words that let us live through it and name it. To carry the world’s pain without breaking, it too needs a form: meaningful, limited contact with the news, a conversation, a cause you take part in.
world_pain.practice: Choose one news story that moved you and give it a form: draw something, light a candle, or do one small good deed. Then put the feed away.

rejection.text: Two lines in an email, and weeks of hurt — Kristeva would explain why this disproportion is no accident. Rejection hurts in the most literal sense, and how deeply it stings doesn’t make you weak. Kristeva named her central idea “abjection,” from the Latin abjectus — “cast off.” She shows that every person, in order to define themselves, casts off whatever doesn’t fit within their boundaries. Kristeva might say that rejection wounds so deeply because it awakens an ancient fear of being cast off oneself. But her analysis says something else too: pushing away is the work of someone else’s boundaries, someone else’s fears, someone else’s history. When you are rejected, it speaks of what the other person needed at that moment, not of what you are worth.
rejection.practice: Put a hand on your own shoulder, the way you would for someone left off the team, and say: “I’m not casting you off.” Hold it for a minute.

abandonment.text: Lullabies are sung so a child can fall asleep without fearing being left — Kristeva believed this fear is older than any words. The fear of being abandoned can go very deep, as if the ground were giving way beneath you, and it doesn’t make you “too dependent.” Kristeva, following psychoanalysis, reminds us that a human being begins in total dependence on others: an infant survives only if it is held and not left alone. This experience doesn’t disappear; it remains in us as the earliest layer. It seems that the fear of abandonment is an echo of that first helplessness, sounding when present bonds feel fragile. But since then you have gathered what the infant didn’t have: words, memory, connections, the experience of having already lived through separations. The adult “I” can hold itself while the fear is sounding.
abandonment.practice: Hold something warm and soft — a blanket, a pillow, a loved one’s sweater — for a minute, feeling that you are being held too.

unrequited.text: Kristeva loved the stories of mystics — Saint Teresa of Ávila, for one, about whom she wrote a novel — people whose love didn’t need to be returned in order to change them. Unrequited love is one of humanity’s oldest stories, and the pain of it is real. In Tales of Love, Kristeva considers love as a work of the imagination: we create an ideal and grow as we reach toward it. She examines the myth of Narcissus, the troubadours who sang of an unattainable Lady, the mystics — and shows that love, even when unanswered, changes the one who loves. Kristeva would probably note that unrequited love is not a pointless waste: in it you discovered in yourself a capacity for tenderness, admiration, an ideal. That capacity is yours; it doesn’t depend on the other’s answer. The pain is still pain. But what awoke in you does not vanish along with the hope of being loved back.
unrequited.practice: Name aloud one quality this love uncovered in you: tenderness, courage, the ability to admire. It stays with you, however the story ends.

humiliation.text: Kristeva would ask not “what is wrong with me” but “whose fragility is this scene covering up.” Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if you had been stripped of your dignity in front of others. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows how people and groups shore up their shaky boundaries by casting someone into the position of the “low,” the “unclean,” the “not like us.” Take Kristeva’s thought one step further, and it turns out that the one who humiliates is often protecting their own fragility: they need someone to be lower in order to feel whole themselves. This doesn’t excuse the one who humiliates, but it clarifies the main thing: the place they tried to put you in is a projection of someone else’s fear, not the truth about you. Your dignity is not created by another’s gaze, and it cannot be revoked by it.
humiliation.practice: Stand up straight, feel your feet and spine, and say your full name aloud to yourself. Dignity lives in the body, and one scene can’t take it away.

body_shame.text: Standards of beauty change every twenty years, but you have only one body — Kristeva would remind us that the “right” body is always invented by culture. Dissatisfaction with your body can be tormenting and draining. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva shows that ideas of a “clean” and “proper” body are created by culture: she examines the biblical purity laws and shows that above all they draw boundaries — what is permitted and what is not. It follows that body shame largely speaks the language of such cultural codes: today’s models of the “right” body are also a system of rules, not nature. But for Kristeva the body is also a source of the semiotic: voice, rhythm, breath, touch, from which our whole life grows. It exists not to be looked at but to be lived in.
body_shame.practice: Slowly stroke your forearm with your palm, from elbow to wrist, the way you’d stroke someone dear. Let your body be not an object of assessment but someone touched with tenderness.

illness.text: For many years Kristeva spoke up for the rights of people with disabilities and wrote that a fragile body doesn’t make a person any less. When your body lets you down, it’s frightening and exhausting, and there is room here for fear, anger and grief alike. In Powers of Horror, Kristeva writes about the “clean and proper” body — the image of a whole, obedient body on which our “I” relies. Illness disrupts this image: the body suddenly turns out to be foreign, unpredictable, as if not quite mine. Kristeva helps us understand why illness wounds not only physically but also your sense of self. At the same time, Kristeva, who wrote a great deal about disability, insisted that vulnerability is not an exception to human life but its common foundation, and it connects people rather than separating them. Your worth does not depend on how well your body works.
illness.practice: Say one sentence to your body, as you would to someone close who is struggling: “I’m with you.” Notice what responds.

pride.text: A child shouting “look what I can do!” doesn’t know the word “modesty” yet — and Kristeva wouldn’t hurry to rein them in. Pride in what you’ve done is a good, well-earned feeling, and you don’t need to hide it. In Tales of Love, Kristeva writes at length about narcissism and, unlike everyday usage, doesn’t consider it a vice. For her, healthy narcissism is the foundation of the psyche: without some love for yourself and your image, you can neither love others nor act. She shows that our “I” is built around an ideal — who we would like to be. Kristeva might say that pride is a moment when you and your ideal briefly meet: what you’ve done matches what you hold dear. Such meetings nourish you and give you strength for the next step. Let yourself feel them fully.
pride.practice: Say aloud, like that child: “Look what I did!” — and name the one detail you’re proudest of.

melancholy.text: Autumn light, an old photograph, a melody that aches — Kristeva knew that loss which has found a beautiful form becomes almost a consolation. Gentle sadness is a state with much depth and beauty in it, and there’s no need to hurry it. Kristeva explores it as an ancient experience of losing something that cannot be named. But the book’s central question is how people turn this sorrow into forms: into paintings, novels, music. For Kristeva, beauty is one such form: it seems to give loss a dignified face and lets it live in us without destroying us. So your gentle sadness is a relative of art: in it, loss has already found a melody. You can stay in it for a while and listen to what it sings.
melancholy.practice: Find an old photograph or a melody that gives you a gentle ache, and stay with it for two minutes. Let loss sound in a beautiful form.

quote.text: My only star is dead, — and my constellated lute bears the black sun of Melancholia.
quote.author: Gérard de Nerval
quote.source: the sonnet “El Desdichado” (1854); this line gave Kristeva’s book Black Sun its title
